name: Sulfur-cured natural rubber
summary: Heating rubber with sulfur made it stay elastic in heat and cold; by 1843 a Connecticut firm was making vulcanized rubber overshoes with the process.
description: Heating natural rubber with sulfur creates sulfur-containing interchain links and changes the material’s temperature-dependent and mechanical behavior; early industrial formulations could also contain other substances.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.
why: Untreated rubber goods turned sticky in summer heat and brittle in winter cold, which limited their use.

market.note: The process can be supplied or used in economic production, separately from the date of its first offer.

evidence.supports: The local historical society reports that Samuel J. Lewis Company began producing vulcanized rubber overshoes at Naugatuck in 1843.
Goodyear’s 1844 patent describes heating a rubber, sulfur and white-lead compound; it does not specify the exact composition of any earlier Lewis shoe.
Describes sulfur crosslinks in natural-rubber vulcanization as a network-forming reaction.
The census account cautiously describes vulcanized metallic rubber shoes as containing sulfur and oven-cured; it does not analyze any individual 1843 Lewis shoe.

date.basis: The Naugatuck Historical Society dates the Lewis company’s vulcanized-overshoe production to 1843.

events.statement: Samuel J. Lewis Company produced vulcanized rubber overshoes in Naugatuck in 1843.
events.scope: Vulcanized rubber overshoes made by Samuel J. Lewis Company.
events.population: Samuel J. Lewis Company rubber-shoe workers
events.caveats: The local account is a retrospective and does not assay a specific 1843 shoe, give an exact sale date, or prove every early manufacturer used Goodyear’s 1844 patent formulation. Older shaped natural-latex goods existed in Mesoamerica; no assertion is made that all such material lacked crosslinks or that ancient individual specimens used a particular additive.
